questions.question: What is the main visual difference between a histogram and a bar chart?
options: Histogram bars touch because the data are numerical and continuous
questions.explanation: A histogram's x-axis is a continuous number line cut into bins, so the bars touch. A bar chart shows separate categories, so its bars have gaps.

questions.question: A long tail stretching to the right means the data are...
questions.explanation: Skew is named after the tail, not the hump. A long right tail means right-skewed (positive skew).

questions.question: In a right-skewed dataset, how do the mean and median compare?
questions.explanation: The few large values in the right tail pull the mean up, while the median resists. Right skew gives mean > median.

questions.question: Tally 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 8, 12 into bins 0-3, 4-7, 8-11, 12-15. What are the frequencies?
Why should you try more than one bin width before interpreting a histogram?
options: The same data can look smooth, jagged or flat depending on the bins
questions.explanation: Bin width changes how the data are grouped. Too wide hides structure and too narrow shows noise. Comparing a few widths protects you from a misleading picture.

questions.question: Which pair should you report for a strongly skewed dataset?
questions.explanation: The median and IQR are resistant to the extreme values that create skew. The mean and SD are pulled around by the tail.
